findings.title: SQL Injection via ORDER BY Parameter
findings.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL commands through the order parameter, allowing unauthorized data read/modification and potential database compromise.
findings.evidence: const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}`, [req.user.id]); — The order variable from req.query.order is directly interpolated into the SQL string without parameterization. Parameterized queries protect values ($1) but not structural elements like ORDER BY columns.
findings.recommendation: Use a whitelist of allowed columns (like the SORTABLE pattern in /payments) and validate order against it: const INVOICE_SORTS = { created_at: true, due_at: true }; if (!INVOICE_SORTS[order]) order = 'created_at';

findings.title: Broken Object-Level Authorization (IDOR) on /invoices/:id
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can read any invoice by guessing its ID, exposing sensitive billing and financial data of other customers.
findings.evidence: const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]); — No WHERE clause checks req.user.id. Compare /receipts/:id on line 14-18 which correctly includes 'AND owner_id = $2' with [req.params.id, req.user.id].
findings.recommendation: Add authorization check: const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2', [req.params.id, req.user.id]); followed by 404 if no rows returned.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in /branding/preview
findings.impact: Attackers can fetch arbitrary URLs, enabling port scanning of internal networks, metadata endpoint access (AWS/GCP credentials), internal API discovery, and potential RCE via confused deputy attacks.
findings.evidence: const image = await fetchLogo(req.body.logoUrl); calls lib/remote.js:5 async function fetchLogo(url) { const response = await fetch(url, { redirect: 'follow' }); } — No URL validation. Accepts any scheme/hostname. The { redirect: 'follow' } option exacerbates the risk by following redirects to internal IPs.
findings.recommendation: Implement allowlist for logoUrl domain: parse the URL, check parsed.hostname against ALLOWED set (lib/remote.js:2). Reject non-http(s) schemes. Set { redirect: 'error' } to prevent redirect-based bypass.

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in invoiceNote Function
findings.impact: If invoice notes are user-editable and rendered in HTML context, attackers can inject JavaScript to steal session tokens, deface content, or redirect users to phishing sites.
findings.evidence:
function invoiceNote(note) { return `
${note}
`; } — The note parameter is directly interpolated without HTML escaping. Contrast with customerName() on line 10 which correctly uses escapeHtml(name).
findings.recommendation:
Apply escapeHtml to the note parameter: return `
${escapeHtml(note)}
`;. If rich HTML is required, use a whitelist-based HTML sanitizer like sanitize-html.

findings.title: JWT Token Accepted Without Cryptographic Verification
findings.impact: Attackers can forge arbitrary JWT tokens with any claims (id, role, tenant) without possessing the signing key, completely bypassing authentication and authorization.
findings.evidence: function currentUser(req) { const claims = jwt.decode(bearer); return { id: claims && claims.sub, role: claims && claims.role }; } — Uses jwt.decode() which only decodes the token payload without verifying the signature. An attacker can create a valid-looking JWT with arbitrary claims.
findings.recommendation: Use jwt.verify(bearer, SECRET_KEY) instead of jwt.decode(). Store the SECRET_KEY securely (environment variable, not hardcoded). Handle verification errors by returning null claims and rejecting the request in middleware.

findings.title: Missing Authorization Middleware on All Endpoints
findings.impact: Endpoints rely on req.user being set by middleware, but there is no visible middleware enforcing authentication. If currentUser() fails silently (returns { id: undefined }), requests proceed unauthenticated.
findings.evidence: Routes use req.user.id without verifying it exists. No Express middleware visible that calls currentUser() and rejects requests if !claims. If a request arrives without Authorization header, jwt.decode(undefined) returns null and claims.sub is undefined.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit authorization middleware before route handlers: router.use((req, res, next) => { req.user = currentUser(req); if (!req.user.id) return res.status(401).json({error: 'Unauthorized'}); next(); });

findings.title: Inconsistent Authorization Logic in /payments Sort
findings.impact: While the whitelist pattern prevents SQL injection, the direct string interpolation is fragile and could be bypassed if the whitelist is modified without updating the parameterization.
findings.evidence: const column = SORTABLE[req.query.sort] || SORTABLE.date; const rows = await db.query(`SELECT * FROM payments WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${column}`, [req.user.id]); — Same anti-pattern as /invoices, even though a whitelist exists.
findings.recommendation: Use parameterized ORDER BY via application logic or a database-agnostic query builder. If raw SQL is required, document the whitelist clearly and add a test ensuring only whitelisted values are ever interpolated.

findings.title: node-fetch Version 2.7.0 May Have Known CVEs
findings.impact: Older versions of node-fetch may contain known security vulnerabilities related to HTTP header injection, DNS rebinding, or request smuggling.
findings.evidence: "node-fetch": "2.7.0" in dependencies. This is an older major version (2.x) of node-fetch. Node.js 18+ has built-in fetch; pinning to 2.x may pull in unpatched vulnerabilities.
findings.recommendation: Run npm audit to identify specific CVEs. Consider upgrading to node-fetch 3.x or using native fetch (Node 18+). If staying on 2.x, apply all security patches and validate against npm advisory database.

findings.title: Unused/Unreachable tagRequest Function with Session Reference
findings.impact: References req.session.user which is never initialized, suggesting incomplete refactoring. May cause runtime errors if called.
findings.evidence: function tagRequest(req, metrics) { ... metrics.increment('requests', { tenant: claims && claims.tenant }); return req.session.user; } — req.session is undefined (no session middleware visible), and the function is exported but not used in the codebase.
findings.recommendation: Remove the function if unused, or clarify its purpose and initialize req.session properly. If session tracking is intended, integrate Express session middleware and document the tagRequest contract.
